chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 321-340: night visits and their dangers on hill and shore (321, 324, 336), the friend's push for disclosure and marriage (321, 332, 333, 339), waiting at evening and midnight while the man crosses the desert for wealth (329-331), his return with the stag at its doe (338), the man's own voice on the embrace and on a girl coming of age (323, 337), and the heroine's laments for a love begun in play or broken by her own word (325, 326, 334, 340).

321.reading: The friend tells the girl that the man who comes at midnight wearing red hill sandal on his chest and a bee-filled garland of spring kuvalai, and then goes back from their house, is her dear companion; now that on the common ground the red-eyed tiger roars after killing the bull of the marai deer, it is no longer a time for hiding, and she will open their door.
321.nuance: The kill is made on the மன்றம், the village's own common ground, so the danger of the night path has come to the door; the friend's 'opening the door' turns secrecy into disclosure, the step toward marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: hill sandal, the tiger and the marai deer of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; she addresses the girl (அரிவை, line 4)

322.reading: The girl tells her friend that, as the soft-eared fawn of the gentle-eyed deer, frightened from its herd when forest folk took it up and brought to the small hamlet by the forest, came to love house life once the youths reared it, nothing is sweeter than what one grows used to; so let them go, walking as they can.
322.nuance: The fawn was taken by force and learned to love the house; she applies it to her own leaving, so the image answers in advance the fear that she cannot live away from her mother's home.

thinai_evidence.note: she resolves to leave home on foot with him

comparisons.tenor: the girl, who will grow used to a new home as the captured fawn did

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; the address தோழி is in line 7

323.reading: The man says all other days are chaff; the only days he has lived are those spent sleeping on the two shoulders of the young woman whose fragrant forehead smells of the pollen of fresh mullai buds blooming in the rain-soaked field, when the thunder rises sweet in the sky like a bards' lute tuned to padumalai.
323.nuance: பதடி வைகல், days of chaff, gives the poet his name; the thunder that in mullai marks the man's promised return here only sweetens the days he has already come back to.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-fed field and the mullai bud

comparisons.tenor: the thunder rising in the rainy sky

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; he speaks as if to himself or a companion

324.reading: The friend tells the man of the great shore, where the crooked-legged male crocodile, strong at seizing, cuts off the paths, that he swims the dark backwater full of fish because of his love and comes, while she suffers because of her innocence, and the friend herself, like one whose twin children have both eaten poison, is afraid in her heart.
324.nuance: The friend splits the situation in three: his love brings him, her innocence makes her suffer, and the fear for both is hers alone; the simile of the twins is what holds the two lovers in one fear.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove and the backwater

comparisons.tenor: the friend, afraid for both lovers at once

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; she addresses him as நீ and பெரும

325.reading: The heroine says that when he kept saying 'I am going, I am going' she took it for one of his old feigned departures and told him to go and stay away for good; alas, where is he now, her lord and support, when the space between her breasts has filled into a great pond where black-legged white herons feed.
325.nuance: She blames herself, not him: the dismissal was hers, spoken in sulking because his departures had been false before; the hyperbole of the heron pond turns the cost of that one word into a landscape.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament after parting, the neythal uri

comparisons.tenor: the tears pooled between her breasts

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker

326.reading: The heroine tells her friend that the love that joined them at the little sand-houses that the broad-shouldered sea-bathing girls with doubled garlands built in the shore grove is such that, if the lord of the shore leaves it for one day, it brings many days of pain.
326.nuance: The love began in a game of house-building on the sand, which makes its fragility literal; the arithmetic of one day against many is the heroine's argument that even a short absence is not small.

thinai_evidence.note: sea-bathing girls and the shore grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker

327.reading: The heroine tells the muddy hill torrent that it is crueller even than the hill lord, who has learnt that it is good to be unkind to the poor ones who live only if he is gracious, for without thinking how soft and pitiable the young girl of their house is, it has brought down a plantain and left the slope bare.
327.nuance: The torrent comes down from his hill, so what it carries to her is a piece of his country; that is why it is crueller than he is: he only neglects her, while it reminds her.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord, the slope and its plantain

comparisons.vehicle: குன்ற நாடன் தன்னினும் நன்றும் நின்னிலை கொடிதால்
comparisons.tenor: the torrent, measured against the man's unkindness

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; she addresses the torrent (கலுழி)

328.reading: The friend says the lord of the shore, where the surf moving with the sound of a drum beaten with a stick ruins the crab's little house in its burrow among the roots of the small-flowered njazhal, was gracious for very few days, yet the gossip is louder than the uproar of Kurumbur on the day the Vicchiyar chief with his bow-armed host fought the kings and bards saw him stand with a tiger's glare.

thinai_evidence.note: njazhal, crab and the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; the man is spoken of in the third person

ullurai.tenor: the man whose brief love has wrecked the girl's good name

pairs.situation: the girl, small and defenceless in her own home
the man's coming, which undoes her good name
the clamour of the gossip that follows

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a crab and surf of the neythal shore in a neythal poem (porul 7.27)

329.reading: The heroine says that thinking of him who crossed the hard desert of towering hills, where white summer flowers of the forest iluppai, shed by long boughs the wind strikes, fall and cover the narrow path where elephants go, she cannot sleep in the thick dark of midnight, and the cold tears come easily to her fine rain-laden eyes like flowers in clear water.
329.nuance: She sees in her mind the path he took, buried under fallen flowers, so the elephant path that should guide him is hidden; the sleepless night is spent on his road.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer desert he crossed

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker

330.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether, in the land he went to, there is no sorrowful evening and its loneliness, when the large-leaved pakanrai opens from its bud a white flower like the thick wick a good washerwoman dipped in starch, lifted and beat and left in the cool pond, and spreads a smell that has nothing of sweet strong toddy.
330.nuance: The question is an accusation: if evening reached his land he would feel what she feels and come home; the scentless flower, white and limp as a starched wick, is the evening of her own field.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting at evening for a man gone away

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker

331.reading: The friend asks whether he will cross the forest of fierce elephants, the waterless hard road where tall bamboo has withered and bowmen with curved bows stand against travellers and plunder the wilds, so that her fine dark body like the tender leaf of the fragrant green mango turns pale, to bring wealth that is hard to win and that he rates above them.
331.nuance: நம்மினுஞ் சிறந்த, better than us, is the sting: the friend states his choice as a ranking in which the women come below the wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless road of withered bamboo

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; the address வாழி தோழி is in line 5

332.reading: The friend asks the heroine what harm there would be if, on this last day of the light rains brought by the north wind, she spoke lovingly to the lord of the hill near the common ground where the great-trunked tusker, embracing his young she-elephant, comes down into the hill hamlet, so that the great anguish of swimming through this sickness may end.

thinai_evidence.note: the tusker and the hill hamlet

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker

iraicchi.act: the tusker, holding his young mate close, brings her down into the hill hamlet by the common ground
iraicchi.sense: as the tusker brings his mate openly into the settlement, the man should take her openly into the village by marriage

333.reading: The friend asks what harm there would be in deciding to reveal their secret, so that the distress of the hill lord's pleading may end: he is lord of the land where the green-eyed elephant, driven off by the hunter with short-shafted arrows and crooked bow after eating the millet field, hangs about the low hillock with the parrots that girls in fragrant leaf-skirts chase away.
333.nuance: கணவும் (line 4) is a rare verb; it is read here as hovering about. The parrots that are driven off with the elephant may also point to the girls' own guarding of the field, but that is not counted as a pair.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field, its parrots and the hill lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; நம் மறை is the secret the two women share

ullurai.tenor: the man who has had the girl's love and is now kept from her

pairs.situation: he has enjoyed her love and is now barred by her guarded house

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses an elephant of the hill millet field in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

334.reading: The heroine asks her friend what else they would lose, if the lord of the wide-watered shore left them, than their own one sweet life: he is lord of the many-flowered grove where the small white red-beaked sea crow, its wet back soaked by the spray of breaking waves, sits sulking at the cold.
334.nuance: The bird sulking (புலந்து) at the cold looks like a lonely lover, but it does nothing that a person of the situation does; it carries a mood only, so it is scene, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: sea crow, waves and the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker

335.reading: The friend says that the village where the broad-shouldered hill girl, sister of hunters with long-shafted strong bows, lives lies close to the hill where bangled girls spread red millet on the wide dark rock and, when they slip off to bathe in the spring, the green-eyed female monkey climbs down the branches and carries it off with her young.
335.nuance: Near miss for ullurai: the monkey watching for the moment the guards slip (சோர்விடை நோக்கி) could match a lover's stealth, and the bow-armed brothers the guarded girl, but neither poem nor colophon states the situation it would point to, so the scene stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: millet, monkey and the hill girl

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; she tells the man where the girl lives

336.reading: The friend asks the lord of the honeyed shore whether one should come like this, painfully, to the delight of enemies, for the girl he left suffers, pitiable, like the neythal of the dark backwater run over by the rim of his long chariot with swift horses while its small-tongued bright bells ring a mournful tune.
336.nuance: The flower is crushed by his own chariot on its way, so the simile lays the harm at his door; 'the delight of enemies' is the gossip of those who are glad to see her fall.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater flower and the lord of the shore

comparisons.vehicle: கடுமா நெடுந்தேர் நேமி போகிய இருங்கழி நெய்தல் போல

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; she addresses him as துறைவ

337.reading: The man says her breasts have budded, her soft gathered hair now hangs down, her close-set white teeth have come in again in order, and a few beauty spots have appeared; he knows she is a stricken power, but she does not know it: what will become of her, the one young daughter of very old rich parents?
337.nuance: The body is catalogued as it changes from child to woman; the man's fear for her (யாங்கா குவள்) is also a fear for himself, since the only daughter of old, rich parents will be hard to win.

thinai_evidence.note: his love is known to him and not to her, one-sided

comparisons.tenor: the girl, as a power that strikes him

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; he speaks to himself

338.reading: The friend says that at the sorrowful evening, when the fine stag with twisted horns, having rested in the shade with his gentle spotted doe and slept in the wide flower-strewn thicket, nibbles the rich green gram as the hour passes, in the cold dewy days at the end of the late dew season, the chariot of great victory has come, so that the loneliness and pallor of the lovely wife of restrained chastity in the bright house may leave.

thinai_evidence.note: stag and doe at evening and the returning chariot

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; she announces the return, perhaps to the household

iraicchi.act: the stag rests with his doe through the day and stays with her into the evening
iraicchi.sense: as the stag stays by his doe at the evening hour, the man has come back to stay with his wife

339.reading: The friend tells the girl that to embrace the fine chest, with its garland of mixed flowers, of the lord of the land where the dense fragrant smoke of akil burned in the wide field drifts off like a cloud with no rain in it and comes down into the kuravar hamlet on the slope, is sweet indeed, but only until it brings tears to her dark kuvalai eyes and pallor.
339.nuance: The smoke that looks like a rain-cloud and gives no rain may shadow a love that promises and brings no marriage; the poem does not draw the match, so it is left as a mood.

thinai_evidence.note: the kuravar hamlet on the slope

comparisons.tenor: the drifting smoke of burnt akil

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; the address வாழி தோழி is in line 5

340.reading: The heroine says that when desire reaches its limit, her heart, longing for her lover yet pitying her and staying with her, cannot settle on either side; like the blossoming kandal standing in the deep water that bends toward where the backwater runs out and turns back when the tide returns, her heart, where he dwells, suffers.
340.nuance: The kandal is rooted: it bends with the ebb and is pulled back by the flood but never leaves its place, which is the heart's state exactly, moving both ways and going nowhere.

thinai_evidence.note: kandal, backwater and tide

comparisons.vehicle: அலர்வேய் கண்டல் கழிபெயர் மருங்கி னொல்கி யோதம் பெயர்தரப் பெயர்தந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: her heart, drawn to him and back to her

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; the address தோழி is in line 7

links.note: Kural 1103 asks whether heaven is sweeter than sleeping on the beloved's soft arms; in Kuruntokai 323 the man calls every other day chaff and counts as lived only the days spent sleeping on her shoulders.
links.teaches: The couplet ranks the embrace above heaven's pleasure; the poem turns the same ranking on time itself, so the pair shows the claim growing from a comparison of joys into a measure of which days of a life count as lived.

links.note: Kural 1192 says a lover's grace to those who love is like rain to those who live by it; Kuruntokai 327's man has learned to withhold grace from those who live only if he is gracious (நல்கின் வாழும்), and water reaches her as a flood from his hill.
links.teaches: Read together, the couplet's rain of grace is shown in reverse: the one who lives by it is denied it, and the water that does come down from the lover's hill is muddy and destroys, so dependence on grace is seen from the side of its failure.

links.note: Purananuru 151 refuses the young Vicchi lord the poet's embrace because of a door shut against singers; Kuruntokai 328 measures gossip by the uproar of Kurumbur when bards saw the Vicchiyar chief stand like a tiger against the kings.
links.teaches: The Vicchi house is remembered by singers in two ways at once, its war-cry loud enough to be an akam poet's yardstick for noise and its door shut against bards in puram, so the pair shows that a chief's fame for valour could circulate apart from, and despite, his name for giving.

links.note: In Kural 1167 the woman swims love's flood without seeing a shore and at midnight is the only one awake; in Kuruntokai 329 she cannot sleep in midnight's thick dark, thinking of the man on the desert road.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the midnight wakefulness as a bare state; the poem gives it a content, the road he took buried under fallen iluppai flowers, so the pair shows the sleepless mind of separation travelling the absent man's road.

links.note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the sad-eyed evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 330 she asks whether the sorrowful evening (புன்கண் மாலை) and its loneliness exist at all in the land he went to.
links.teaches: Both make the evening testify against the absent man, but in opposite ways: the couplet makes it a fellow sufferer, the poem imagines a land without it, which would explain why he stays away, so the pair shows the evening serving as companion and as accusation.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 63 the man's heart argues that work for wealth must be pressed because the penniless can neither give nor enjoy; in 331 the friend says he goes for wealth he rates above them (நம்மினுஞ் சிறந்த).
links.teaches: The same journey for wealth is a duty in the man's reckoning and a ranking of the women below gold in the friend's, so the pair shows that the paalai departure is argued from both houses and that neither side's account mentions the other's.

links.note: In Kural 1155 the woman tells her friend to prevent the departure of the one fit for her, since once he goes union is hard; in Kuruntokai 334 she tells her friend that if he leaves, what they lose is only their one life.
links.teaches: Both speak to the friend before a parting, but the couplet asks for help to stop it while the poem asks for none and names the price, her life, so the pair shows the same plea in two moods, one still bargaining and one already resigned.

links.note: In Kural 1081 the man cannot tell whether she is an anangu, a peahen or a woman; in Kuruntokai 337 he is sure she is an anangu (அணங்கென) and adds that she herself does not know it.
links.teaches: The couplet's bewilderment is about what she is; the poem moves it to the gap between her power and her ignorance of it, the one-sided love of kaikkilai, so the pair shows the anangu figure turning from a lover's confusion into an observation about a girl not yet aware of herself.

links.note: In Akananuru 34 the returning man sees a stag feed and guard its doe and hurries his chariot home; in Kuruntokai 338 the friend sets a stag resting with its doe at evening beside the news that the victorious chariot has come.
links.teaches: The stag with its doe is the spur to return in the man's mouth and the sign that the return has happened in the friend's, so the pair shows one iraicchi working at both ends of the journey, as motive and as fulfilment.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 65 the stag back with its mate in the rains mocks the waiting woman because her man has not come; in 338 the same pairing at evening comes with the chariot that ends her pallor. On the waiting woman's reading in 65 the sign is false; in 338 it is kept.
links.teaches: The same image of the stag beside its mate is read as a reproach when the man fails the season and as a promise kept when he arrives, so the pair shows that the iraicchi carries no fixed sense apart from whether the man returns.

links.note: In Kural 1249 the woman asks her heart whom it goes seeking, since the lover is within it; in Kuruntokai 340 her heart, where he dwells, can settle on neither side and sways like a kandal with ebb and tide.
links.teaches: The couplet treats the heart's going out to him as an absurdity to point out; the poem's rooted kandal, bent out by the ebb and back by the flood, makes the same divided heart a rhythm she cannot stop, so the paradox becomes a condition rather than an error.

links.note: The line ஆசா கெந்தை யாண்டுளன் கொல்லோ closes the friend's memory of how he won the girl in 176 and stands in 325 after the heroine admits she herself told him to go.
links.teaches: The same cry for the lost support carries blame of the man in the friend's poem and self-reproach in the heroine's, so the pair shows a formula line taking its charge from who speaks it and what precedes it.

source_issues: 321 to 340: the colophon thurai names only the speaker (தோழி கூற்று and the like), so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem; each item says so in its note.
332: the colophon thinai is பாலை (sangamtamil.com gives குறிஞ்சி, as the flag says); the poem is all hill (யானை, குன்றச் சிறுகுடி, மலைகிழவோன், வாடை), marked kurinji.
336: the colophon thinai is குறிஞ்சி (sangamtamil.com gives நெய்தல், as the flag says); the poem is all shore (துறைவ, இருங்கழி நெய்தல்), marked neythal.
324 line 6: கவைமக (the twin child) is a rare figure, and the poet is named after it; the simile is read as fear for two at once and the verse is marked uncertain.
325 line 4 (ஆசா கெந்தை யாண்டுளன் கொல்லோ) repeats Kuruntokai 176 line 5; its first words are hard to divide, read as 'my lord who was my support'.
333 line 4: கணவும் is a rare verb, read as hovering about; marked uncertain.
329 line 7 (TSCII repair), 331 line 5, 337 lines 3 to 5 and 338 line 5 are repaired readings, as show flags; they read correctly.
330: the colophon thinai is மருதம்; the karu is of the watered fields, but the situation is a wife waiting at evening for a man gone to another land, marked mullai.
338: the colophon thinai is பாலை; the poem is the man's return at evening with a stag and doe, marked mullai.
